title: Back-of-the-Envelope Estimation
oneLine: Turn vague scale into a few defensible numbers: peak QPS, storage growth, bandwidth, cache size, partitions, and headroom.
opening: Before choosing technology, I would translate the product assumptions into order-of-magnitude capacity. I will state every assumption, round numbers deliberately, and calculate average QPS, peak QPS, write volume, storage growth, network throughput, and likely cache working set. I am not trying to predict production exactly; I am checking whether the design needs one machine, tens of machines, or a globally partitioned system. I would then use those estimates to justify the number of partitions, database choice, queue throughput, and retention tiers, and I would call out the two or three assumptions to validate with real measurements.
ask: How many actions per user per day and what is the read/write split?
What is the average and p95 payload size?
What peak multiplier and retention period should we design for?
scale: Peak QPS = average QPS × an explicit peak factor.
Storage/year = writes/sec × bytes/write × 31.5M seconds × replication factor.
Bandwidth = requests/sec × bytes/request; calculate ingress and egress separately.
Cache target = hot-object count × bytes/object × overhead, not the whole database.

decisions.default: Use one or two significant digits and powers of ten.
decisions.why: Interview estimates are for architecture classification, not a finance forecast.
decisions.switch: Use exact values only when checking a hard protocol or bit-allocation boundary.

decisions.default: Design critical paths for peak and long-running storage for average plus growth.
decisions.why: Daily averages hide open-of-market, celebrity, launch, and regional spikes.
decisions.switch: Use burst queues when the business allows deferred processing instead of provisioning every worker for instantaneous peak.

decisions.default: Include copies, indexes, metadata, and encoding overhead.
decisions.why: Logical payload size can understate physical storage by several times.
decisions.switch: For rough first pass, state a 2–4× multiplier and refine only if the design hinges on it.

deepDives.title: Useful mental constants
points: A day is about 10^5 seconds; a year about 3×10^7 seconds.
1 KB × 1M events is roughly 1 GB; 1 KB × 1B events is roughly 1 TB.
Network and storage units may use decimal while memory often uses binary; say which approximation you use.

deepDives.title: Sensitivity analysis
points: Show what changes if payload grows 10× or peak grows 5×.
Identify the dominant term rather than refining insignificant ones.
Use a range when the product assumption is genuinely uncertain.

failures.response: Calculate average and at least one peak scenario; name the product event that creates the peak.
Apply an explicit physical-storage multiplier and state what it covers.
Write units beside every number and convert once, visibly.
Round early and give a range; say which assumption matters most.

questions.q: How many servers do we need?
questions.a: First estimate peak work and define a safe per-instance capacity from load tests, then divide and add N+1/AZ-failure headroom. CPU is only one constraint; include memory, connection pools, and downstream limits.
Estimate the working set, not the full dataset. Start with the objects responsible for perhaps 80–95% of reads, include Redis/object overhead, and confirm with hit-rate curves in production.

questions.q: What if the estimate is wrong?
questions.a: Design for observability and elastic partitioning. The purpose of the estimate is to avoid a category error; runtime metrics and load tests replace assumptions as soon as the system exists.

questions.q: How do estimates influence database choice?
questions.a: They expose write rate, data volume, access pattern, retention, and consistency needs. Those decide whether one relational primary is enough, whether partitioning is required, and whether a log/column/time-series store fits better.

mistakes: Starting arithmetic before clarifying product behavior
Choosing a database from user count alone
Spending ten minutes optimizing a number that cannot change the architecture
seniorSignal: Use the estimate to make a decision: ‘This fits one primary,’ ‘we need 32 partitions,’ or ‘egress dominates cost.’ Numbers without a design consequence are noise.
implementation: Use the built-in calculator on this site during practice
Turn assumptions into load-test scenarios and per-instance SLOs
Capture real p95 payloads and peak multipliers once telemetry exists
